transcription.tex: \textbf{Improper integrals}\par Replace an infinite limit or an undefined endpoint with a limit.\par Check convergence before evaluating.
\textbf{Further techniques}\par Find the mean value of a function.\par Differentiate and integrate inverse trigonometric functions.\par Use partial fractions in integration.

transcription.tex: 1. Why does direct substitution give an impossible result for \(\int_{-1}^{1}x^{-2}\,dx\)?
\[[-x^{-1}]_{-1}^{1}=-2\]This is invalid: the integrand is undefined at zero. Split the integral there. Each positive part diverges, so the improper integral diverges.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Infinite intervals}\par An integral can converge even though its interval is unbounded. For example, the normal density has total area 1:\[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^2/2}\,dz=1\]Always check that each required limit exists.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: A function tending to zero is not sufficient for its integral to converge.\par Similarly, the harmonic series \(\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}1/r\) diverges despite its terms tending to zero.

slides.title: The Mean Value of a Function

transcription.tex: \textbf{Mean value of a function}\par The discrete mean is \((y_1+\cdots+y_n)/n\). For equally spaced samples, a limiting average gives:
\[\overline f=\frac1{b-a}\int_a^bf(x)\,dx\]The integral is the signed area; divide by the interval width.\par A constant function has that same constant as its mean.

transcription.tex: Why does the gradient joining the first and last points give the average rate of change?\par Apply this to water cooling from \(80^\circ\mathrm C\) between \(t=0\) and \(t=800\).
\[\overline{f^{\prime}}=\frac1{b-a}\int_a^bf^{\prime}(t)dt\]\[=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}\]This is exactly the secant gradient. The average rate of decrease is \((80-T(800))/800\).

transcription.tex: 10. Sketch each composite inverse trigonometric function, giving its domain and range.
Odd and increasing; passes through the origin.\par Domain \([-\sin1,\sin1]\); range \([-\pi/2,\pi/2]\). Vertical tangents at both endpoints.
Increasing from \((\cos1,0)\) to \((1,\pi/2)\).\par Domain \([\cos1,1]\); range \([0,\pi/2]\). Vertical tangents at both endpoints.
Odd and increasing through the origin.\par Domain \(\mathbb R\); range \((-\arctan(\pi/2),\arctan(\pi/2))\). These bounds are horizontal asymptotes.
